utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, I'm here with David Cunningham and Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. So let's -- anything before bringing in the witness? All right. So we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. I promised you Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman that I would hand down the substance of the decision on the fresh motion for the subpoena of Jonathan Randal. Our decision --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's in open session but this is technically there is a confidential -- I think Your Honour will have to do a public motion eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact it's part of the decision is to lift the confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I'm specifying that first. And then I can proceed. So the part of the decision is precisely that there is no reason why the decision itself and all the proceedings relating to it ought to remain confidential. They are -- confidentiality is being lifted. The second and main part of the decision is that the motion is being rejected and the third part is that the article itself is being admitted in evidence, with the usual caveat that the -- whether the -- whether any probative value or any value at all would be given to it will be decided later on during the Chamber's final deliberations. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it, Your Honour, that full reasons for these decisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will be included in the written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Will be included in the written judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly and the reason why the written judgement is not being handed down today is that there is a divergence of opinion on a part of the decision, of the decision, not on the decision itself, on the decision we are fully and unanimously in agreement but we are deliberating whether to incorporate it in the decision itself or have it come forward as a separate opinion explaining the -- one particular aspect which does not affect the decision itself but it's part of the reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, I'm told by Mr. Ackerman, I have not yet seen it, but that he's filed a formal motion raising the same point that he raised yesterday in respect of the Glas article but in writing. I don't know whether Your Honours have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I have not seen it, no. No, we haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know how much effect that will have on any ruling or indeed what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a motion, please reply it to it ASAP and we will decide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When we get it Your Honour we're having -- at the moment we are only told it has been filed nothing has been given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't seen it either. Yes, Mr, Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just my typical objections to various exhibits in the Celinac batch. I mentioned it to you yesterday, I mentioned that I had trouble getting it faxed to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see but that's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there is no formal motion. It's just my objections and I think you've primarily ruled upon them. I don't think the Prosecutor probably needs to respond unless they feel they need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is obviously a misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I understood from Mr. Ackerman when I asked him this morning that he had filed a specific motion in respect of the non-admittance of newspaper articles because they are in breach of Rule 92 bis. And that's wrong is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not going to tell you that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not wrong. It's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I think we probably have to formally respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We decided it yesterday, Ms. Korner. I said that I considered this indeed novel but quite incomprehensible submission of law. That's how I consider it. And that's -- we gave a decision accordingly. It was a very short oral decision that we completely disagree with his submission and that's it. I don't think you need to respond. If later on there is a formal motion putting more flesh, then we obviously go into it and I would imagine that we will willy-nilly have to come to this at some point in time later on during submissions because there are several documents that Mr. Ackerman I would expect would continue objecting to and stress and make submissions upon so our position is a very simple one. I mean we are adopting the procedure that has been adopted so far in practically all the other trials pursuant also to some of the decisions of the Appeals Chamber, that more or less unless on the face of it, a document is absolutely unacceptable and inadmissible from the very word go, we admit it with the usual caveat, and basing ourselves later on on the various principles regulating evidence, we will see what importance if at all to attach to these documents, particularly although not exclusively had they happened to be newspaper articles so -- but it's -- we are not excluding giving newspaper articles any importance. We might. There were some newspaper articles this morning, for example, which might carry some weight, considering the rest of the evidence or might not be given any weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Before I re-raise the matter I think I'll wait for Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner. Microphone for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll await Your Honours decision on this and the reason that you give for refusing the witness summons. Your Honour, may I just add a word of caution. The public version will of course be very careful to avoid any reference to matters that were confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have taken that into consideration again, as well, I mean that's why I started precisely with the confidentiality, the annex, if I remember well, will remain -- it has been taken care of, Ms. Korner already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if before it's -- if it's before it goes to the press, we could be kind enough for it not to be released immediately to the press until we've had a look at it. We are just a little concerned because there was a genuine reason for the confidentiality aspect because if you're releasing our motion which we have no objection to, save in so far as there was reference to matters which should remain confidential so we'd just like to check it before the public version goes out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that, giving a copy to Mr. Ackerman as well, with the understanding that it will be kept for your eyes only until we then make it public, okay? I have your word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I just wonder if you would consider at page 66, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I have to go to page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 66, line 1. I wonder if you would consider striking the word incomprehensible as a description of my submission. I think it was comprehensible, you just rejected it. It's embarrassing to be publicly described as someone making incomprehensible submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I really thought about it, Mr. Ackerman, but if it irritates you, I take it back, I take it back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour think it wise to take the break now before bringing the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. How long do you expect this witness to last on direct, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A few hours, Your Honour. I won't finish him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no chance of going through his statement and asking him whether he would confirm --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I discuss it with Ms. Korner at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If Mr. Ackerman is prepared for the cross-examination, perhaps we could finish him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The only problem Your Honour, I wanted to put a number of documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's taken for granted but he's a pretty straightforward witness in the sense that I'm not saying that there is nothing in his statement that is or may not be controversial but it's the kind of statement that perhaps when one -- one could adopt with additional questions and of course supporting documents, and then perhaps if Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Cunningham, I don't know who would be cross-examining him, hasn't got much time, or doesn't envisage a lengthy cross-examination, any way, could you discuss it amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did discuss the matter with the Defence during the break and we both agree that we would rather take the witness as we normally do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When I said a few hours I mean possibly two. I don't think it's going to be a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have areas where perhaps it will be shorter and more practical to refer straight to the statement, go there. I'm not asking for the statement to be exhibited or be tendered an exhibit, instead, or in lieu of the testimony. That's not what I'm asking but certain parts can be read out and we cut what could become a long story quite short.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll also be referring to Exhibits P2052, 62, 63 and 64 which don't appear on that proposed exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me jot them down. Today or on Tuesday when we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning -- or good afternoon to you, sir. You are Mr. Jadranko Saran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are a witness in the proceedings, in the trial that has been instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin, and very shortly you will start giving your testimony. Our rules require that before you do so, you enter, you make, a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that the usher, Madam Usher is handing to you now. Please read it out, aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair, a seat. Considering who you are, I don't think I need waste time to explain to you the procedure. Ms. Sutherland will start with her examination-in-chief. And she will be followed by Mr. Cunningham with his cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin. That won't happen today. I suppose it will be on Tuesday. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: My name is Jadranko Saran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on the 19th of November, 1958, in Sokolac in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of November, 1959, in Stolac, in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation came through as 1959. Were you born in 1958 or 1959?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to go through some background information, your background information. If you could just answer yes or no when I put the question to you we will move a little bit faster. Is your father's first name Hadze?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Hadze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your ethnicity is Bosniak and your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You graduated from the University of Mostar in 1983 majoring in economics? Sir, you need to respond for the -- into the microphone so that it gets picked up to be put on to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After finishing university, you worked in Stolac as an economist until 1987 when you moved to Bosanska Krupa municipality?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you took up a position there as an economist in the Kombitekst, the textile factory, as chief import/export services? Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 1st of September, 1991, you were appointed as the deputy commander of the police station in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you applied for that post?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father a policeman?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained in this position as deputy commander of police until the 25th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you currently hold the position of chief of police in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position do you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: I am a company manager of a company called Kemokomerc, in a canton.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the canton, Usko-Sanski canton, the canton of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are married with two children?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some stage become the chief of police in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that position for and when was it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Almost eight years. From April, 1994, until November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move now to ask you a few questions about the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P60? Sir, this is a record of the 1991 census figures. Could I ask you to go to Bosanska Krupa, which is on page 3 of the document, midway down the page? We can see that the 1991 results, there were 58.320, that was the total population. And of that number, 43.104 were of Muslim ethnicity, 13.841 were Serbs, there were 139 Croats, and 1.236 declared themselves as Yugoslav or other? In other words, this is a municipality where the overwhelming majority was of Muslim ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your own experience, that was true?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate percentages of the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: 76 per cent were Muslims, Bosniaks, and 24 per cent approximately Serbs, and 2 per cent of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P56? Sir, after the events which occurred in the municipality in April, 1992, which we will discuss a little later, you remained in the municipality, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at that document? It consists of figures compiled by the Banja Luka CSB in May, 1993. We can see for Krupa na uni that approximately 43.300 Muslims had moved out by May, 1993, and approximately 4.760 Serbs and 143 Croats? And we can see from this document that the data for the number of Serbs moving in was not available. Could you tell the Court briefly where all the Muslim residents went?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Well, this is the document done by the security services centre in Banja Luka. It is probably true. All Muslims, Bosniaks, that were in the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa after the war broke out, they escaped, that is they were expelled to the left bank of the Una River to a free territory, while the Muslim enclaves that remained on the right bank of the Una River, Muslims inside of them were captured and later on deported, either towards the Bihac area or further away abroad, by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a map of the ethnic composition of Bosanska Krupa? This is a new exhibit, Your Honour, and if it can be provisionally marked as P2020? If that map could be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with the pointer that's just in front of you, the silver pointer, could you take that and point on the ELMO machine to your right and just explain to the Judges what you meant a moment ago when you spoke about the left and the right bank?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: In the town of Bosanska Krupa is divided by the Una River, as a kind of natural border. On two parts. There is the right bank of the Una River, of the Bosanska Krupa town is more urban settlements. That's the urban part of town. And then there is the left bank of the Una, that is of Bosanska Krupa, and you can see on the ELMO that it is in green colour that the areas were marked where the Muslims had majority, in terms of the population, while it was in other colours that the area was marked in the areas where Serbs were the majority, had the majority population. The right bank of the town of Bosanska Krupa and the Muslims who were on the right bank, on the right side, after the war broke out, they managed to cross to the left bank, to the left side, while on the right-hand side, there is only Muslim enclaves that were left, Veliki Dubovik, Arapusa, Ostroznica, Mali Badic and Veliki Badic. This population was blocked by the Serbs, and they couldn't get out to the left side, to the left bank of the Una River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, pause there. We will go into more detail in relation to that a little later in your testimony. Just for now, so you've mentioned the towns, the Muslim towns that were on the right bank. Can you tell Their Honours, for example, is the town of -- the village of Ljusina, Prstaline, Jezerski, are they all -- they are all the Muslim villages on the left side of the bank? The left bank?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the village of Perna, can you point to that? And is that misspelled on this map. It should be P-E-R-N-A?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: P-E-R-N-A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown another map of the Bosanska Krupa municipality? And it could be provisionally marked P2021.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this map here shows the municipality in full and it also shows the other municipalities that surround it, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've finished with that map for the moment. I want you to look at some photographs which appear on that -- on P2021. Actually just while you've got it there. Can you tell the Judges what is depicted in photograph number 1?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Arapusa, the village of Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour in order to save time that is also depicted in photograph P2113.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir what is depicted in photograph number 2?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: The photograph number 2 is depicting the Petar Kocic primary school and its sports hall, its gym.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For Your Honours and the Defence that is photograph number P2113.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir what is shown in photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the village on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your pointing to the village of Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Petar Kocic elementary school is in Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: No. The Petar Kocic school is in the centre of the town of Bosanska Krupa, near the hospital, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. And Your Honour was wanting to you points on the map where the Petar Kocic school was. What is shown in photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: That is the outside-view of the same school, Petar Kocic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours and the Defence that is P2113.6. Sir, finally what is shown in photograph number 4 on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Photograph number 4 is the village of Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which particular building in the village of Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is P2113.7. Can you point to the village of Jasenica on the map?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with those maps -- that map, thank you. Sir, are you aware of any military installations that were in the Bosanska Krupa municipality?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: There were no military installations in the Bosanska Krupa municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the nearest installations?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: The nearest installations were in Bihac, Petrovac, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn to another topic now. Have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was elected as president of the municipal assembly after the 1990 elections, who became the president?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: You mean of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Mehmet Mahic, his name was Mehmet Mahic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the head of the TO in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Hasim Djulic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want to turn to the police. Who was the chief of the police before the war?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Semso Velic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Laza Stupar, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the commander of the police in charge of?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: The commander of the police was in charge of the uniformed policemen, and the person who was in charge of the use of police, it's through him that all the orders went, but as far as the chief of police is concerned, he was the head of the uniformed police as well as of the administration while the commander of the police was the one who commanded the police in uniform and issued orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Mile Mudrinic, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court the ethnic composition of the police in Bosanska Krupa in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: The ethnic composition in 1991 looked like this: 60 to 70 per cent at least members of the police were Serbs. The rest were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the composition change, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: In March, 1992, there was more of a balance, as far as the ethnic composition of the police is concerned, and there were more policemen who were Muslims, that is Bosniaks, and they were given the chance to become employees of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: I am saying that the majority in February or March, that's when the balance, there was much more of a balance, but already in 1991, October, November, what was then also present was the -- more of an increased employment of Muslims, Bosniaks. That's when this process of balancing began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, may I please butt in here? In your statement, on page 3, you don't need to see it, but I can read out to you, you say, "It was not until February or March, 1991 that the ethnic composition of the police started to become more balanced with more Bosniaks and less Serbs being recruited." Is it correct February or March, 1991, or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because until now he's been referring to February, March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've cleared it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what was the relationship like between the Serbs and the Bosniaks prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that change in any way? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Things changed. That could have happened already in 1991, when the Serbs wanted to establish a community of Serb municipalities of Krajina. It was from then that they put everything into this objective for the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, they were -- they established the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. From then on, that's when the animosity started to develop and increase between Bosniaks and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also an incident that occurred in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes. In September, 1991, in the Bosanska Krupa municipality, that is in Bosanska Otoka, Milan Martic was arrested together with a general, I do not recall the name of the general, and a driver. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Martic released or was he kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: That day, when Martic was arrested, that is he had been recognised by citizens on the iron bridge in Bosanska Otoka he was stopped at the checkpoint and after that he was arrested and transferred to the police department in Bosanska Otoka. He was kept that night and the following day, he was released following the intervention of the federal Ministry of the Interior and a gentleman who had come, he was the deputy Minister of the Interior, Avdo Hebib.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, sir, what was the ethnicity of the police who stopped and detained Mile Martic at the checkpoint in Bosanska Otoka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several policemen. I -- at the moment I can't tell you exact what their ethnicity was, but what happened was the citizens recognised Mr. Martic in the car because there was an arrest warrant in Croatia for -- that was issued for him, and that's why he was detained at the police department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I accept that at the moment you can't tell exactly what their ethnicity was, but taking into consideration that at the time the ethnic composition in the police force was -- still showed a majority of Serbs, would you say that the composition of that -- of the police group at that checkpoint would be also predominantly Serb when they arrested Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That was the police detachment in Bosanska Otoka was mixed. There were both Serbs and Muslims but who was at the checkpoint at the time I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, go ahead, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for completeness, who is Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Mile Martic was the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the organiser of the rebellion in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the Krajina in Bosnia or the Krajina in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that relations changed between the Serbs and the Bosniaks when the Serbs wanted to create their own municipality?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before we go on to that, after Martic's release, did something happen at the police station, the Bosanska Krupa police station?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes. First time it happened that policemen of Serb nationality, that is for the first time in Bosnia-Herzegovina that it happened, that the policemen of Serb ethnicity simply all went to the village of Jasenica taking the weapons and vehicles with them, those vehicles they had access to. They remained in the village of Jasenica, establishing their own police station, i.e., only Serb police station, and they established some checkpoints. Since this is the first time that it happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a team from the federal Ministry of the Interior that came from Sarajevo and representatives of the union, they all came to Bosanska Krupa, trying to convince the Serbs that they should return to the mother station and continue their work. They couldn't get through with official vehicles because of the roadblocks, so they had to use a helicopter to go to the village of Jasenica, they had their discussions and returned. And then after about seven days, the Serbs returned to the police station of Bosanska Krupa and started to work together with the rest again, but that was not just -- just ordinary work. It then became obstructive work by the Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to another topic and that is to do with the arming of the Serbian population. Are you aware of whether -- how, if and when Serbs were armed within the municipality of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: In 1991, that was the year when the Serbs started to arm themselves in a systematic fashion through the Yugoslav People's Army. Very frequently we received the information and intelligence, and they were corroborated later, that there had been vehicles, Pinzgauer vehicles, in the only-Serbs areas and they were bringing different types of weapons and ammunition, and those weapons and ammunition were left in those villages and Serb areas, one of the examples is the village of Perna on the left bank of the Una river, where it was on several occasions that a helicopter landed, bringing weapons to this Serb village. And then the weapons were distributed to the people there. Since that was an enclave on the left bank of the Una river, and a Serb enclave among the Muslims, it was not possible because that's not what the administration, political administration wanted. The search, it was not possible to conduct it because in that case there would have been cause for another incident. They were armed also through other means and channels and almost all of them in the areas of the right bank of the Una river, almost all of them had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the weapons in the TO?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: The weapons at the Territorial Defence, most of the weapons, by a JNA order, they were moved to a warehouse in Svodna near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any of these weapons ever returned to the municipality of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the weapons were returned, was returned, but it is perhaps that 50 per cent of the weapons returned were unoperational. There were parts of the weapons which were non-existent on the rifles, so most of the weapons were non-operational, which means that this had been done on purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear that the weapons had first of all been taken from the warehouse and then about the weapons that had been returned?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO SARAN
utterances.text: Chief Mr. Velic, who is the chief of police, had close cooperation with the Territorial Defence. The chief of Territorial Defence, Mr. Hasim Djulic and, of course, with the chief of the municipality. So it was at a meeting that Mr. Velic told us, informed us, that the weapons from the Territorial Defence had been transferred to Svodna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sutherland. And thank you. Mr. Saran, I suppose it has been explained to you that we wouldn't have finished with your testimony today and that you would have to stay over the weekend plus Monday, which is a United Nations holiday, and that you will continue with your testimony on Tuesday, when hopefully we should be in a position to conclude. So I wish you a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same for Mr. Cunningham and Ms. Sutherland and the rest. We stand adjourned until Tuesday, 9.00 in the morning. Ms. Chuqing will be circulating to you -- you have already done that? Asking for your go ahead to move sittings in one week in July and some other days to -- from the afternoon to the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, we have absolutely no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you perhaps may need to consult with Ms. Korner, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But as soon as you can confirm to Madam Chuqing your addition to this suggestion, then we can move ahead. Thank you. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
